Hot is to cold as up is to ___
Hot and cold are opposites; so are up and down.
Which word does NOT belong? apple, banana, carrot, grape
Apple, banana and grape are fruits; a carrot is a vegetable.
Bird is to nest as bee is to ___
A bird lives in a nest; a bee lives in a hive.
Which word does NOT belong? river, lake, ocean, mountain
River, lake and ocean are bodies of water; a mountain is a landform.
Pen is to write as knife is to ___
A pen is used to write; a knife is used to cut (tool and function).
Author is to book as composer is to ___
An author creates a book; a composer creates a song.

Which word does NOT belong? sprint, jog, stroll, whisper
Sprint, jog and stroll are ways of moving; whisper is a way of speaking.
Drought is to water as famine is to ___
A drought is a shortage of water; a famine is a shortage of food.
Which word is the OPPOSITE of "scarce"?
"Scarce" means hard to find; the opposite is plentiful.
Glove is to hand as sock is to ___
A glove covers a hand; a sock covers a foot.
Which pair has the same relationship as "pebble : boulder"?
A pebble is a small stone and a boulder a large one; a puddle is small water and a lake large water.
All roses are flowers. Some flowers are red. Which MUST be true?
["All roses are red.","Some roses are red.","No roses are red.","None of these must be true."]
Nothing says the red flowers are roses, so none of the statements must be true.
Which word is closest in meaning to "ephemeral"?
"Ephemeral" means lasting only a short time, i.e. brief.
Candid is to frank as cautious is to ___
"Candid" and "frank" are synonyms; so are "cautious" and "wary".

The teacher said: "Please open your books to page twelve and read the first paragraph quietly."
What should the students do first?
["Close their books","Open their books to page twelve","Talk to a partner","Write a story"]
Key line: "The teacher said: "Please open your books to page twelve and read the first paragraph quietly." So the answer is "Open their books to page twelve".
Sam says: "I'm hungry. I want an apple and a glass of milk."
["An apple and milk","Bread and juice","Pizza","Water only"]
Key line: "I want an apple and a glass of milk." So the answer is "An apple and milk".
Announcement: "The school library will close early today at two o'clock because of a meeting. Please return your books before then."
Why will the library close early?
["It is a holiday","There is a meeting","The books are missing","It is raining"]
Key line: "Announcement: "The school library will close early today at two o'clock because of a meeting." So the answer is "There is a meeting".
Lena tells her friend: "I couldn't come to practice yesterday because my little brother was sick, so I stayed home with him."
["She was tired","She forgot","Her brother was sick","She had a test"]
Key line: "Lena tells her friend: "I couldn't come to practice yesterday because my little brother was sick, so I stayed home with him." So the answer is "Her brother was sick".
The science teacher explains: "Plants make their own food using sunlight, water, and air. This process is called photosynthesis."
["A way plants make food","A kind of weather","A type of soil","A way animals sleep"]
Key line: "The science teacher explains: "Plants make their own food using sunlight, water, and air." So the answer is "A way plants make food".
Coach: "We'll meet at the north gate, not the main entrance. The bus leaves at eight, so please don't be late."
["At the main entrance","At the north gate","On the bus","In the gym"]
Key line: "Coach: "We'll meet at the north gate, not the main entrance." So the answer is "At the north gate".
A guide says: "Please stay with the group, and do not touch the exhibits. If you have a question, raise your hand."
What should visitors do if they have a question?
["Touch the exhibit","Leave the group","Raise their hand","Wait outside"]
Key line: "If you have a question, raise your hand." So the answer is "Raise their hand".
Radio: "Tomorrow will start cloudy, but by afternoon the clouds should clear and the temperature will rise to twenty-five degrees."
What will the weather be like tomorrow afternoon?
["Rainy and cold","Clear and warmer","Cloudy all day","Snowy"]
Key line: "Radio: "Tomorrow will start cloudy, but by afternoon the clouds should clear and the temperature will rise to twenty-five degrees." So the answer is "Clear and warmer".
Teacher: "Although the experiment failed, we learned that the metal expands when heated, which is useful information."
["The experiment was perfect","Metal expands when heated","Metal melts at once","Heat is dangerous"]
Key line: "Teacher: "Although the experiment failed, we learned that the metal expands when heated, which is useful information." So the answer is "Metal expands when heated".
Speaker: "Contrary to popular belief, goldfish can remember things for months, not seconds, which is why they can be trained to recognize feeding times."
What is the speaker's main point?
["Goldfish have poor memories","Goldfish can remember for months","Goldfish dislike feeding","Goldfish cannot be trained"]

Key line: "Speaker: "Contrary to popular belief, goldfish can remember things for months, not seconds, which is why they can be trained to recognize feeding times." So the answer is "Goldfish can remember for months".
Tom has a red ball. He plays with it at the park every day after school.
Where does Tom play with his ball?
["At school","At the park","At home","At the beach"]
Key line: "He plays with it at the park every day after school." So the answer is "At the park".
Rosa planted seeds in a small pot. She watered them every morning. After two weeks, tiny green leaves appeared.
["The pot broke","Green leaves appeared","Rosa stopped watering","The seeds disappeared"]
Key line: "After two weeks, tiny green leaves appeared." So the answer is "Green leaves appeared".
The class went to the zoo. They saw lions, monkeys, and a very tall giraffe. Everyone liked the monkeys best.
Which animal did everyone like best?
Key line: "They saw lions, monkeys, and a very tall giraffe." So the answer is "Monkeys".
Recycling means turning old things into new things. When we recycle paper, fewer trees are cut down, and less energy is used.
What is one benefit of recycling paper?
["It makes more trash","Fewer trees are cut down","It costs more energy","It makes paper heavier"]
Key line: "When we recycle paper, fewer trees are cut down, and less energy is used." So the answer is "Fewer trees are cut down".
Because the river flooded last spring, the villagers built a wall of stones along its bank. Since then, the houses have stayed dry.
Why did the villagers build the wall?
["To make a road","To stop the river flooding their homes","To catch fish","To start a market"]
Key line: "Because the river flooded last spring, the villagers built a wall of stones along its bank." So the answer is "To stop the river flooding their homes".
Volcanoes form where hot melted rock, called magma, rises through cracks in the Earth's crust. When pressure builds up, the magma can erupt as lava.
What causes a volcano to erupt?
["Heavy rain","Pressure from rising magma","Strong wind","Ocean waves"]
Key line: "When pressure builds up, the magma can erupt as lava." So the answer is "Pressure from rising magma".
The word "transparent" means that light can pass through something so you can see clearly. Glass windows are usually transparent.
Which object is most likely transparent?
["A wooden door","A glass window","A brick wall","A metal box"]
Key line: "Glass windows are usually transparent." So the answer is "A glass window".
Although the festival was small when it began, word of mouth gradually drew visitors from neighbouring towns, and within a decade it had become the region's most anticipated event.
What can be inferred about the festival?
["It stopped after ten years","It grew because people told others","It was always large","It only had local visitors"]

Key line: "Although the festival was small when it began, word of mouth gradually drew visitors from neighbouring towns, and within a decade it had become the region's most anticipated event." So the answer is "It grew because people told others".

Some people think students should wear uniforms; others disagree. Write a paragraph giving your opinion with at least two reasons.
Introduce yourself. Say your name, your age, and two things you like to do. (Record for about 30 seconds.)

When the town planted trees along Maple Street, many residents complained about the cost. Ten years later, the shade lowered summer temperatures by several degrees, and neighbours began gathering under the branches each evening. The mayor admitted that the trees had paid for themselves in ways no budget could measure.
What is the mayor's attitude toward the trees by the end of the passage?
He admits they paid for themselves.

The mayor admitted that the trees had paid for themselves in ways no budget could measure.
Which sentence best states a theme of the passage?

According to the passage, what happened ten years later?

Scientists studying coral reefs have noticed that reefs near busy harbours often recover more slowly after storms. The researchers suspect that pollution weakens the coral, but they caution that more data is needed before the cause can be confirmed.
Which word best describes the researchers' conclusion?
"Suspect" and "more data is needed" signal caution.

Scientists studying coral reefs have noticed that reefs near busy harbours often recover more slowly after storms. The researchers suspect that pollution weakens the coral, but they caution that more data is needed before the cause can be confirmed.
What does "caution" mean as used in the passage?

What is the passage mainly about?

The wind is given a human action.
Choose the correct word: "They ___ going to the zoo."
Which sentence begins with a capital letter and ends correctly?
["we like pizza.","We like pizza.","We like pizza","we Like pizza?"]
Choose the correct plural: one child, two ___
Which word completes the sentence? "She ran ___ than her brother."
Which sentence is in the past perfect tense?
["I eat lunch.","I had eaten lunch before she arrived.","I will eat lunch.","I am eating lunch."]
Choose the correct possessive: "The ___ toys were everywhere."
Which sentence contains a misplaced modifier?
["She nearly drove her kids to school every day.","She drove her kids to school every day.","Every day, she drove her kids to school.","She drove her kids to school daily."]
"Nearly" should modify "every day" or be placed differently.
Which is the best transition: "The experiment failed. ___, the team learned something useful."
Day is to night as summer is to ___
Day and night are opposites; so are summer and winter.
Which word does NOT belong? dog, cat, horse, chair
Dog, cat and horse are animals; a chair is furniture.
Eye is to see as ear is to ___
The eye is used to see; the ear is used to hear.
Which word means the same as "huge"?
Chapter is to book as scene is to ___
A chapter is a part of a book; a scene is a part of a play.
Which word is the OPPOSITE of "generous"?
"Generous" means giving; the opposite is selfish.
Which word does NOT belong? triangle, square, circle, cube
Triangle, square and circle are flat (2-D); a cube is solid (3-D).
Thermometer is to temperature as ruler is to ___
A thermometer measures temperature; a ruler measures length.
All birds have feathers. A penguin is a bird. Which MUST be true?
["A penguin has feathers.","A penguin can fly.","All feathered animals are birds.","Penguins live in cold places only."]
Penguins are birds and all birds have feathers, so penguins have feathers.
Which word is closest in meaning to "ambiguous"?
"Ambiguous" means open to more than one meaning, i.e. unclear.
Prudent is to reckless as frugal is to ___
"Prudent" is the opposite of "reckless"; "frugal" is the opposite of "wasteful".
Anna says: "My birthday is on Saturday. I'm having a party at my house."
["At school","At her house","At the park","At a restaurant"]
Key line: "I'm having a party at my house." So the answer is "At her house".
Teacher: "Tomorrow is picture day. Please wear your school shirt and bring your homework."
Key line: "Please wear your school shirt and bring your homework." So the answer is "Their school shirt".
Dad: "We're out of milk, so I'm going to the store. Do you need anything?"
Why is Dad going to the store?
["To buy milk","To meet a friend","To return a book","To get gas"]
Key line: "Dad: "We're out of milk, so I'm going to the store." So the answer is "To buy milk".
Principal: "The assembly will begin at ten, but students from Room 4 should arrive early to help set up chairs."
Key line: "Principal: "The assembly will begin at ten, but students from Room 4 should arrive early to help set up chairs." So the answer is "Students from Room 4".
Ranger: "Because the trail is muddy after the rain, we will take the lower path, which is longer but safer."
Why will the group take the lower path?
["It is shorter","It is safer","It has a view","It is closed"]
Key line: "Ranger: "Because the trail is muddy after the rain, we will take the lower path, which is longer but safer." So the answer is "It is safer".
Lecturer: "Although electric cars produce no exhaust, their overall environmental benefit depends on how the electricity is generated."
["Electric cars are always clean","Benefits depend on the electricity source","Exhaust is harmless","Electric cars are expensive"]

Key line: "Lecturer: "Although electric cars produce no exhaust, their overall environmental benefit depends on how the electricity is generated." So the answer is "Benefits depend on the electricity source".
Mia has a cat named Pepper. Pepper likes to sleep on the sofa and drink milk.
What does Pepper like to drink?
Key line: "Pepper likes to sleep on the sofa and drink milk." So the answer is "Milk".
On Monday, the class started a garden. They planted beans, carrots, and corn. Each student has a job.
What did the class start on Monday?
Key line: "On Monday, the class started a garden." So the answer is "A garden".
The library offers free programs during the summer. Children can join a reading club, and older students can volunteer as helpers.
Key line: "Children can join a reading club, and older students can volunteer as helpers." So the answer is "Older students".
Rain forests are home to millions of species. Many of these plants and animals cannot live anywhere else on Earth.
["They are cold","They shelter species found nowhere else","They have no animals","They are small"]
Key line: "Rain forests are home to millions of species." So the answer is "They shelter species found nowhere else".
The inventor tested hundreds of materials before finding one strong enough. "Every failure," she said, "taught me what not to do."
What does the inventor's statement show?
["She gave up easily","She learned from failures","She disliked testing","She worked alone"]
Key line: "Every failure," So the answer is "She learned from failures".
Economists note that when a product becomes scarce, its price typically rises unless demand falls at the same time.
What usually happens to the price of a scarce product?
["It falls","It rises","It stays the same","It disappears"]
Key line: "Economists note that when a product becomes scarce, its price typically rises unless demand falls at the same time." So the answer is "It rises".
Describe what you do on a typical weekend. Use at least five sentences and words like "first", "then", and "finally".
Talk about your favorite food. What is it, how is it made, and why do you like it? (Record for about 45 seconds.)

Which word does NOT belong with the others? apple, banana, carrot, grape
Carrot is a vegetable while the others are fruits.
Which word belongs with the group: dog, cat, rabbit?
Dogs, cats and rabbits are pets and hamster is also a pet animal.
Bird is to nest as bee is to ?
A nest is where a bird lives and a hive is where bees live.
Which word means the same as happy?
Glad is a synonym of happy.
Which word is the opposite of hot?
Cold is the antonym of hot.
All dogs are animals. Rex is a dog. Which statement MUST be true?
["Rex is an animal.","Rex is a cat.","All animals are dogs.","Rex is not an animal."]
Rex belongs to the group dogs, and every dog is an animal.
Which word does NOT belong with the others? Monday, Friday, July, Sunday
July is a month while the others are days of the week.
Hand is to glove as foot is to ?
A glove is worn on the hand and a sock is worn on the foot.
Which word means the same as rapid?
Rapid and quick both mean fast.
Which word is the opposite of ancient?
Ancient means very old and modern means of the present time.
All roses are flowers. All flowers need water. Which statement MUST be true?
["Some roses do not need water.","Roses need water.","Roses are the only flowers.","All plants are roses."]
Roses are flowers and all flowers need water, so roses need water.
Which word belongs with the group: triangle, square, pentagon?
All are flat shapes with straight sides, and a hexagon is another one.
Which word does NOT belong with the others? violin, cello, flute, harp
The violin, cello and harp have strings but the flute is a wind instrument.
Author is to novel as composer is to ?
An author creates a novel and a composer creates a symphony.
Which word means the same as reluctant?
Reluctant means not wanting to do something, which is unwilling.
Which word is the opposite of scarce?
Scarce means in short supply and plentiful means available in large amounts.
No fish are mammals. All whales are mammals. Which statement MUST be true?
["All fish are whales.","All mammals are whales.","No whales are fish.","Some whales are fish."]
Whales are mammals and no mammal is a fish, so no whale is a fish.
Which word does NOT belong with the others? scissors, knife, saw, spoon
Scissors, knife and saw are used for cutting but a spoon is not.
Thermometer is to temperature as barometer is to ?
A thermometer measures temperature and a barometer measures air pressure.
Which word means the same as meticulous?
Meticulous means showing great attention to detail.
Which word is the opposite of generous?
Generous means giving freely and stingy means unwilling to give.
Some students in the club play chess. All students who play chess are in Year 7. Which statement MUST be true?
["No Year 7 students play chess.","All club students are in Year 7.","All Year 7 students are in the club.","Some club students are in Year 7."]
The club members who play chess are in Year 7, so at least some club students are.
Which word does NOT belong with the others? cautious, prudent, wary, reckless
Reckless means careless of danger while the others mean careful.
Drought is to water as famine is to ?
A drought is a shortage of water and a famine is a shortage of food.
Eulogy is to praise as satire is to ?
A eulogy is meant to praise and satire is meant to mock.
Which word means the same as ephemeral?
Ephemeral describes something that lasts only a very short time.
Which word is the opposite of benevolent?
Benevolent means well-meaning and malicious means intending harm.
No reptiles are warm-blooded. Some pets are reptiles. Which statement MUST be true?
["No pets are warm-blooded.","Some pets are not warm-blooded.","Some warm-blooded animals are reptiles.","All pets are reptiles."]
The pets that are reptiles cannot be warm-blooded.
Mia is taller than Noor. Noor is taller than Omar. Pia is shorter than Omar. Who is the second tallest?
The order is Mia, Noor, Omar, Pia, so Noor is second.
Which word does NOT belong with the others? verbose, wordy, prolix, laconic
Laconic means using very few words while the others mean using too many.

A fish moves by swimming and a bird moves by flying.

Select the word whose meaning is closest to HUGE.
Huge means extremely large, as enormous does.
Select the word whose meaning is closest to FRUGAL.
Frugal means careful about spending money.
Select the word whose meaning is closest to RELUCTANT.
Select the word whose meaning is closest to CANDID.
Select the word whose meaning is closest to MEAGER.
Meager means small in amount, like scanty.

Obsolete means no longer in use, or outdated.
Select the word whose meaning is closest to BENIGN.
Benign means gentle or not harmful.

Tenacious means holding firmly, or persistent.

Eloquent means fluent and persuasive in speech, or articulate.
Select the word whose meaning is closest to PRUDENT.
Prudent means showing good judgment, or sensible.

The puppy was so ___ after the long walk that it fell asleep immediately.
Falling asleep right away suggests the puppy was exhausted.
Because the road was icy, the driver proceeded ___.
Ice calls for careful, cautious driving.
The soup was so ___ that she added more salt.
Adding salt makes sense only if the soup lacked flavor.
Despite her ___ appearance, the old dog was surprisingly strong.
Despite and surprisingly signal a contrast with strong, so frail fits.
The author's ___ prose made even the simplest idea easy to follow.
Lucid means clear, which makes ideas easy to follow.
The hikers were ___ by the sudden storm, but their guide remained ___.
But signals contrast between the hikers' alarm and the guide's calm.
The mayor's speech was deliberately ___; no one could tell whether she supported the plan.
If no one could tell her position, the speech was unclear or ambiguous.
Because the museum's funds were ___, the curators had to ___ several planned exhibits.
Limited money would force the curators to cancel exhibits.
Her ___ remarks hurt his feelings, though she insisted she had meant no harm.
Hurtful remarks made without intent to harm were thoughtless.
The explorer's ___ nature drove him to seek out every unmapped valley.
Seeking unmapped places shows an adventurous nature.
The critic was usually ___, so her ___ praise of the film astonished readers.
Astonishment implies a harsh critic gave unexpectedly enthusiastic praise.
The detective's ___ attention to detail allowed him to notice what others overlooked.
Noticing what others miss requires meticulous, extremely careful attention.
The tyrant's ___ rule left the citizens with no voice in their own government.
A tyrant who denies citizens a voice rules in a despotic way.
The ___ heat of the desert made travel ___ during the afternoon.
Scorching heat would make afternoon travel grueling.
The professor's ___ lecture, filled with obscure references, left most students more confused than before.
Abstruse means hard to understand, matching the confusion described.
Though the diplomat's manner was ___, her proposals were ruthlessly firm.
Though signals contrast, so a friendly (affable) manner contrasts with firm proposals.
Not content with ___ praise, the ambitious young poet craved ___ acclaim.
An ambitious person unsatisfied with modest praise would crave universal acclaim.
Her ___ response to the crisis, neither panicking nor hesitating, earned her the board's trust.
Neither panicking nor hesitating describes a measured response.

Every morning, Marisol climbed the narrow stairs to her grandfather's workshop, where dozens of clocks ticked out of step with one another. As a small child she had found the noise maddening, but now she barely heard it. Her grandfather, bent over a brass gear no larger than a coin, never looked up when she entered. "Hand me the tweezers," he would say, and she would, and that was their entire conversation until noon. Yet she had come to understand that this silence was not coldness. It was the way he welcomed her: by assuming she belonged there. When a customer once asked why such a quiet girl bothered to visit, her grandfather answered without lifting his eyes. "She is the only one who knows when to stay still," he said. Marisol pretended to polish a clock face, but her cheeks burned with pride.
What is the passage mainly about?

["A girl's growing appreciation of her grandfather's quiet way of showing acceptance","A customer's complaint about a clock repair","A child's frustration with a noisy workplace","The history of clockmaking in a small town"]
The passage traces how Marisol comes to see her grandfather's silence as welcome.

Octopuses are masters of disguise, but the mechanism behind their transformations is stranger than most people realize. Beneath an octopus's skin lie thousands of tiny sacs of pigment called chromatophores, each surrounded by muscles. When the animal wants to change color, its brain signals the muscles to stretch the sacs open or squeeze them shut, altering the pattern across its body within a fraction of a second. Remarkably, octopuses appear to be colorblind; their eyes contain only one type of light-sensing cell. Researchers therefore puzzle over how the animal matches its background so well. One hypothesis is that the skin itself contains light-sensitive proteins that detect surroundings directly, allowing the octopus to "see" with its body. Although the idea remains unproven, laboratory studies have shown that isolated patches of skin react when exposed to light, lending the theory some support.
Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?

["Octopuses are the most intelligent sea animals.","Laboratory research is more reliable than field research.","Colorblind animals cannot hide from predators.","Octopuses change color using pigment sacs, yet how they match their backgrounds remains puzzling."]
The passage explains the color mechanism and then raises the open question.

When the animal wants to change color, its brain signals the muscles to stretch the sacs open or squeeze them shut, altering the pattern across its body within a fraction of a second. Remarkably, octopuses appear to be colorblind; their eyes contain only one type of light-sensing cell. Researchers therefore puzzle over how the animal matches its background so well. One hypothesis is that the skin itself contains light-sensitive proteins that detect surroundings directly, allowing the octopus to "see" with its body. Although the idea remains unproven, laboratory studies have shown that isolated patches of skin react when exposed to light, lending the theory some support.
Why do researchers find the octopus's ability to match its background puzzling?
["Its skin contains no pigment","It rarely changes color","Its brain is unusually small","Its eyes seem unable to perceive color"]
The animal appears colorblind yet matches colors well.

Before the Erie Canal opened in 1825, shipping a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City cost about one hundred dollars and took weeks of jolting travel by wagon. The canal, a 363-mile waterway dug largely by hand, cut that cost to roughly ten dollars and shortened the trip considerably. Farmers in the Midwest suddenly found that their grain could reach eastern markets profitably, and they planted more. Towns such as Rochester and Syracuse grew rapidly along the route, and New York City surpassed rival ports to become the nation's busiest. Not everyone benefited, however. Farmers in New England, facing cheaper western produce, struggled to compete, and many abandoned their land for factory jobs or for the West itself. The canal thus illustrates how a single improvement in transportation can reshape the economy, creating winners and losers at the same time.

["The Erie Canal reshaped the economy, helping some regions while hurting others.","The Erie Canal was the longest waterway ever built.","Wagon travel was safer than canal travel.","New England farmers invented new crops."]

Translators are often described as invisible, and the best are said to be those whose work readers never notice. Yet this ideal is more contested than it appears. A translator who renders a novel into smooth, natural English may erase the strangeness that made the original distinctive; the foreign rhythms, unfamiliar idioms, and odd turns of phrase are, after all, part of what the author intended. Some contemporary translators therefore deliberately preserve awkwardness, trusting readers to tolerate friction in exchange for authenticity. Critics reply that a translation no one can comfortably read has failed its audience as surely as one that distorts the original. The disagreement is unlikely to be settled, because it reflects a genuine tension between two loyalties: fidelity to the author and service to the reader. Every translator, in effect, must choose where to stand between them.

When a honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers, it returns to the hive and performs a "waggle dance" to share the news. The bee shuffles in a figure-eight pattern, vibrating its abdomen during the straight middle section. The angle of this waggle run, measured against the vertical wall of the comb, tells the other bees which direction to fly relative to the sun. The length of the run indicates distance: the longer the waggle, the farther away the food. Observers in dark hives have confirmed that the bees follow these instructions with surprising accuracy, even when the sun is hidden behind clouds. Scientists consider the dance remarkable because few animals other than humans communicate information about things that are not present.

Seventeenth-century Dutch painters turned away from the grand religious and mythological scenes that had dominated European art. Instead, a rising merchant class wanted pictures of their own world: a woman pouring milk, a tavern crowded with card players, a quiet street after rain. Such works were modest in scale, since they were meant to hang in ordinary homes rather than cathedrals. Yet their apparent simplicity is deceptive. Painters labored over the fall of light on a copper pot or the texture of a linen cloth, convinced that attention to the everyday could reveal something enduring. Some scholars read hidden moral lessons into these scenes, such as warnings against idleness or excess. Others argue that the paintings celebrate ordinary life for its own sake. Probably both views contain some truth, for the artists seldom explained themselves.
According to the passage, why were these paintings modest in scale?
["Churches forbade large canvases.","Painters lacked skill.","Paint was scarce.","They were meant to hang in ordinary homes."]
The passage says they were meant for ordinary homes rather than cathedrals.

The shop smelled of oil and old paper, and Mara had stopped noticing either by the third week. Her grandfather worked at the bench beneath the window, a loupe screwed into one eye, his breath slowed to the rhythm of whatever movement lay open before him. He did not speak while he worked, and at first Mara had taken his silence for disapproval. She had arrived in June with a suitcase and a sullen certainty that the summer was a punishment.

On Thursday a woman brought in a mantel clock wrapped in a bath towel. It had belonged to her mother, she said, and it had not run in eleven years. Her grandfather lifted it from the towel the way one might lift a sleeping cat.

"Will it be expensive?" the woman asked.

"It will be slow," he said, which was not an answer, though the woman seemed to accept it as one.

After she left, he slid the clock across the bench toward Mara. She stared at it. In three weeks he had let her sort screws, wind finished pieces, and sweep. He had never let her open anything.

"The case first," he said. "Then you tell me what you see. Not what you think. What you see."

Mara reached for the smallest screwdriver, and her hand, she noticed, was not quite steady.

Every spring, mayors across the country pose with shovels beside freshly planted saplings, announcing goals of ten thousand or a million new trees. The photographs are pleasant, and the ambition is sincere. Yet the obsession with planting obscures a less glamorous truth: a young street tree is a liability before it becomes an asset. In its first three years, it needs regular watering, staking, and protection from mowers and road salt. Without that care, a significant share of newly planted trees in some cities die before they ever cast meaningful shade.

Mature trees, by contrast, deliver benefits that saplings cannot match for decades. A single large oak intercepts far more stormwater, cools far more pavement, and filters far more air than a dozen thin saplings planted in its place. Yet when a sidewalk needs repair or a utility line needs space, the old tree is often the first thing removed, because replacing it with a sapling counts as "no net loss" on a city's spreadsheet.

Cities should therefore measure their urban forests not by how many trees they plant but by how much canopy they sustain. That shift would redirect money toward maintenance crews, watering programs, and engineering solutions that let sidewalks and roots coexist. It would make for duller ribbon cuttings. It would also make for cooler, greener streets.

The author's concluding paragraph explicitly argues that cities should measure success "not by how many trees they plant but by how much canopy they sustain."

To the Honorable Council of the Town of Ashford Mills,

Gentlemen,—I have this week completed the survey you commissioned regarding the proposed extension of the canal to the northern quarries, and I must, in candor, report that the undertaking is neither so simple nor so cheap as the petition laid before you has represented. The petitioners estimate the cost at eleven thousand dollars. I cannot, in good conscience, place it below nineteen.

The difficulty lies chiefly in the ground itself. Beyond the second mile, the soil gives way to a broken shale which will not hold water without lining, and the lining alone will consume a sum the petitioners have omitted entirely. Moreover, the rise toward the quarries requires not two locks, as they suppose, but four.

I do not write to discourage the enterprise. The quarries are rich, and a waterway would reduce the cost of hauling stone by more than half, to the lasting benefit of every merchant in the town. I write only so that the Council may decide with its eyes open rather than be persuaded by figures that will not survive the first season of digging. An honest estimate disappoints once; a dishonest one disappoints every quarter until the work is abandoned.

I remain, Gentlemen, your obedient servant,
Josiah Whitcombe, Engineer
What is Whitcombe's main purpose in writing this letter?

["to correct an unrealistically low cost estimate while still supporting the project if it is honestly funded","to persuade the Council to reject the canal extension entirely","to request payment for the survey he has completed","to accuse the petitioners of attempting to defraud the town"]
He states that the petitioners' figures are too low but adds, "I do not write to discourage the enterprise," showing he wants an informed decision rather than a rejection.

Lichens look like little more than crusty stains on rocks and bark, but they are among the most sensitive living instruments scientists possess. A lichen is not a single organism but a partnership: a fungus provides structure and shelter, while an alga or cyanobacterium supplies food through photosynthesis. Because lichens have no roots and no waxy outer layer, they absorb water and nutrients directly from the air—and, with them, whatever pollutants the air carries.

This vulnerability makes lichens useful. Species differ sharply in their tolerance for sulfur dioxide and nitrogen compounds. Shrubby, branching lichens tend to vanish first as pollution increases, while flat, crusty species persist in dirtier conditions. By surveying which forms grow on trees in a given area, researchers can estimate air quality without installing expensive monitoring equipment.

The method has limits. Lichens grow slowly, so a survey reflects conditions over years rather than days; a sudden spike in pollution may not register at all. Local factors such as humidity and bark acidity also influence which species thrive, so a sparse lichen community does not automatically indicate dirty air. Researchers therefore treat lichen surveys as a complement to instrument readings, not a replacement—an inexpensive way to map broad patterns and identify places where closer monitoring is warranted.
Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?

["Lichens consist of a single organism that has adapted to polluted air.","Lichens are dangerous to trees because they absorb pollutants from the bark.","Lichens' sensitivity to pollutants makes them useful, though imperfect, indicators of long-term air quality.","Lichen surveys have replaced expensive air-monitoring instruments in most cities."]
The passage explains why lichens reveal air quality and then outlines the method's limits, presenting lichens as a valuable but imperfect tool.

Tidewater

Twice a day the river forgets which way it runs.
The salt comes shouldering up from the bay,
patient as a creditor, and the brown water
turns back on itself as if remembering
some errand it left undone upstream.

My grandmother said the marsh keeps two clocks:
one for the sun, one for the moon,
and that a person raised here learns to read both—
when to set the crab pots, when the mud
will hold a boot and when it will keep it.

I have stood on bridges in other cities
and watched the current slide beneath me, sure
and single, carrying its leaves away,
and felt almost sorry for it, never once
asked to turn around.

I live inland now, where rivers know their minds.
They hurry one direction, plain as a sentence.
But some nights, lying awake, I feel it still:
the slow pull backward, the long hesitation,
the water deciding, again, to come home.
The simile describing the salt water as "patient as a creditor" suggests that the tide

["moves quickly and unpredictably through the river","returns steadily and inevitably, as if to collect what it is owed","is weak compared with the force of the river","is generous to the people who live along the marsh"]
A creditor waits calmly but always comes back to collect, which mirrors the tide's slow, certain return twice a day.

With four hundred meters left, Dev was in fifth place, and fifth place did not qualify for anything.

He had run this race in his head a hundred times on the drive up, and in every version he had made his move at the final curve, sweeping past the leaders with a grace he had never actually possessed. Popular history loves a solitary genius. We picture the inventor alone in a workshop at midnight, struck by inspiration that no one else could have summoned. The image flatters our sense of drama, but it distorts how discovery actually happens. Nearly every celebrated breakthrough was preceded by years of incremental work by people whose names have faded, and many were reached almost simultaneously by rivals working independently—a sign that the idea was, in a sense, ready to be found.

This matters for more than historical accuracy. When students absorb the myth of the lone genius, they learn to see talent as a lightning strike that either hits them or does not. Those who struggle conclude that they simply lack the spark, and they quit. Meanwhile, institutions that believe in lone geniuses pour resources into identifying a few stars rather than building the collaborative environments in which most good ideas actually emerge.

None of this means individuals do not matter; some people do see further or work harder than their peers. But we should tell the story of discovery as it usually unfolds: as a relay rather than a sprint, with each runner carrying the baton a little further before handing it on.

For much of the twentieth century, sleep was regarded as a kind of shutdown—a period when the brain, like an idle engine, simply rested. Research over the past several decades has overturned that view. During sleep, and especially during the deep, slow-wave stages that dominate the early part of the night, the brain appears to replay patterns of activity first generated during waking experience.

In studies with rodents, scientists recorded neurons in the hippocampus, a region involved in forming memories, while animals explored a maze. Later, as the animals slept, the same neurons fired in the same sequences, often compressed into a fraction of the original time. Disrupting these replay events tended to impair the animals' performance when they returned to the maze the next day.

Human studies point in a similar direction. Volunteers who learn a list of word pairs and then sleep typically recall more of them than volunteers who spend the same interval awake. Some experiments have even played faint sounds associated with specific learned material during deep sleep and found that the cued items were remembered better.

Researchers caution that much remains uncertain. Replay has been observed most clearly in animals, and the precise mechanisms linking it to human memory are still debated. Still, the evidence has decisively retired the idle-engine metaphor.

The passage describes the overturning of the "idle engine" view and presents evidence for memory replay while noting that mechanisms are still debated.

Mangrove forests grow where few other trees can survive: in salty mud that is flooded twice a day by the tide. Their tangled roots rise above the waterline like stilts, allowing the trees to take in air even when the soil beneath them contains almost none. Some species also pump excess salt out through their leaves, which can be seen as white crystals on sunny afternoons. These adaptations are only part of the story. The roots slow incoming waves, so sediment settles and builds up new land over time, and the sheltered water among them serves as a nursery for young fish. Scientists once assumed that the sleeping brain simply rests. Experiments with volunteers have since overturned that view. In one study, participants learned a list of word pairs and were then divided into two groups: one slept for eight hours, the other stayed awake. When tested the next day, the sleepers recalled roughly 20 percent more pairs. Brain scans suggest why: during deep sleep, patterns of activity from the day are replayed, apparently strengthening the connections that store new information. Researchers caution that sleep is not a substitute for study; a student who never reviews material has nothing for the brain to replay. Still, the results make all-night cramming look like a poor bargain.
What is the main idea of the passage?
["Sleep helps the brain strengthen new memories.","The brain rests completely during sleep.","Volunteers dislike memory experiments.","Students should avoid studying."]
The passage reports that sleep boosted recall by strengthening connections.

An octopus has no shell and no bones, yet it survives in waters full of hungry predators. Its best defense is camouflage. Special cells in its skin, called chromatophores, can expand or shrink in a fraction of a second. Each cell holds a tiny sac of color, so the octopus can turn from red to brown to nearly white as it moves across a reef. Some octopuses also change the texture of their skin, raising small bumps to look like rough rocks or seaweed. Scientists once believed the animal relied on its eyes to match its surroundings. However, recent studies suggest that the skin itself may sense light, helping the octopus blend in even when parts of its body are hidden from view. If camouflage fails, the octopus can squirt a cloud of dark ink and escape.

Beginning more than two thousand years ago, a network of trade routes known as the Silk Road linked China with the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. Few merchants traveled the entire distance. Instead, goods passed from trader to trader, and each handoff raised the price. Silk, spices, and paper moved westward, while glass, gold, and horses traveled east. Yet merchandise was not the only thing that crossed these deserts and mountains. Ideas, religions, and even diseases moved along the same paths. Buddhism, for instance, spread from India into East Asia largely through travelers on these roads. Towns along the way, such as Samarkand, grew wealthy by providing food, water, and shelter to caravans. Historians therefore describe the Silk Road not merely as a place for buying and selling but as a meeting point of cultures.

When a honeybee finds a rich patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and performs a figure-eight dance on the honeycomb. The straight middle part of the dance, called the waggle run, carries the message. The angle of the run, measured against gravity, tells the other bees which direction to fly relative to the sun. The length of the run indicates distance: the longer the waggle, the farther the flowers. Researchers who first decoded the dance in the 1940s were astonished, because it suggested that insects could share precise information symbolically. Later experiments strengthened that view. When scientists moved a food source while a hive's dancers were advertising its old location, bees that followed the dance arrived at the empty spot and searched there, which showed that they were relying on the dancers' directions rather than simply smelling the food.
What does the length of the waggle run tell other bees?
["How many bees should go","How far away the flowers are","Which flower is the largest","How sweet the nectar is"]
The passage says a longer waggle means farther flowers.

Before canals, farmers in inland regions often struggled to sell their crops. Wagons were slow, roads turned to mud in the rain, and a heavy load of grain could cost nearly as much to haul as it was worth. Then a canal was dug linking the interior to the coast. Leaves look green in summer because they contain chlorophyll, a pigment that captures sunlight for making food. As days grow shorter in autumn, trees stop producing chlorophyll, and the green fades. The yellow and orange colors that remain were present all along; they were simply hidden. Red leaves are different. Their color comes from anthocyanins, pigments that many trees manufacture only in autumn, from sugars trapped in the leaves. Bright, sunny days and cool nights produce the richest reds, because sunshine builds up sugar while cold prevents it from leaving the leaf. In a cloudy, warm autumn, the display is usually duller. Brown leaves, finally, result from waste products left behind after the other pigments are gone.
Why do yellow and orange colors appear in autumn?
["Cold air changes green leaves to yellow.","They are produced from trapped sugars.","Trees make them from sunlight in October.","They show once the green chlorophyll fades."]
Those colors were present all along but hidden by chlorophyll.
